title: Definition 1.1 — Proposition
Example 1: Identifying Propositions
content:
Classify each of the following as a \textbf{proposition} or \textbf{not a proposition}.
If it is a proposition, state its truth value.

\vspace{0.3cm}
\textcolor{primaryblue}{\textbf{Solution:}}

\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{tabular}{|p{6cm}|c|c|}
\hline
\rowcolor{primaryblue!20}
\textbf{Sentence} & \textbf{Proposition?} & \textbf{Truth Value} \\
\hline
``Islamabad is the capital of Pakistan.'' & \textcolor{darkgreen}{\checkmark} Yes & True \\
\hline
``$2 + 2 = 5$'' & \textcolor{darkgreen}{\checkmark} Yes & False \\
\hline
``What time is it?'' & \textcolor{red}{$\times$} No & --- \\
\hline
``Close the door!'' & \textcolor{red}{$\times$} No & --- \\
\hline
``$x + 1 = 5$'' & \textcolor{red}{$\times$} No & --- \\
\hline
``Every even number greater than 2 is the sum of two primes.'' & \textcolor{darkgreen}{\checkmark} Yes & Unknown \\
\hline
``The moon is made of cheese.'' & \textcolor{darkgreen}{\checkmark} Yes & False \\
\hline
\end{tabular}

\vspace{0.4cm}
\textcolor{accentorange}{\textbf{Note:}} ``$x + 1 = 5$'' is \textbf{not} a proposition because its truth value depends
on the value of $x$ — it is called a \textbf{predicate} (covered in Section~1.4).
The Goldbach conjecture (last row) is a proposition even though mathematicians have not
yet proved or disproved it; it is still either true or false.

Example 3: Translating English to Symbolic Logic
content:
Let $p$ = ``It is raining'' and $q$ = ``She will go to college.''
(This exact example appeared in \textbf{Past Paper 2021 Q1(ix)}.)

\vspace{0.3cm}
\textcolor{primaryblue}{\textbf{Solution:}}

\vspace{0.3cm}
Express each English sentence symbolically:

\vspace{0.2cm}
\begin{tabular}{|p{7cm}|c|}
\hline
\rowcolor{primaryblue!20}
\textbf{English Sentence} & \textbf{Symbolic Form} \\
\hline
It is raining. & $p$ \\
\hline
It is not raining. & $\neg p$ \\
\hline
It is raining and she will go to college. & $p \land q$ \\
\hline
It is raining and she will \textbf{not} go to college. & $p \land \neg q$ \\
\hline
It is raining or she will go to college. & $p \lor q$ \\
\hline
If it is raining, she will go to college. & $p \rightarrow q$ \\
\hline
She will go to college if and only if it is raining. & $q \leftrightarrow p$ \\
\hline
\end{tabular}

\vspace{0.3cm}
\textcolor{accentorange}{\textbf{Note:}} The answer to Past Paper 2021 Q1(ix) is
$\boxed{p \land \neg q}$.

Theorem 1.1 — Logical Equivalence of Conditional
content:
For any propositions $p$ and $q$:
\[
    p \rightarrow q \;\equiv\; \neg p \lor q
\]
That is, the conditional ``if $p$ then $q$'' is logically equivalent to
``not $p$ or $q$''.

Definition 1.13 --- Contingency
content:
A compound proposition is called a \textbf{contingency} if it is \textbf{neither a
tautology nor a contradiction} --- that is, it is true for some assignments and false
for others.

\vspace{0.3cm}
\textbf{Example:} $p \land q$ is true when both are T, and false otherwise.
It is a contingency.

Theorem 1.2 --- Tautology and Contradiction Relationship
Proof of Theorem 1.2
content:
\textcolor{primaryblue}{\textbf{Proof:}}

\textbf{Step 1: Setup.}

Let $\varphi$ be a compound proposition containing variables $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$.
Suppose $\varphi$ is a tautology, meaning for every truth-value assignment
$\mathcal{A}$ to $p_1, \ldots, p_n$:
\[
    \mathcal{A}(\varphi) = \mathbf{T}
\]

\textbf{Step 2: Evaluate $\neg\varphi$ under any assignment.}

Let $\mathcal{A}$ be any truth-value assignment. By the definition of negation:
\[
    \mathcal{A}(\neg\varphi) = \mathbf{T} \iff \mathcal{A}(\varphi) = \mathbf{F}
\]
Since $\varphi$ is a tautology, $\mathcal{A}(\varphi) = \mathbf{T}$ for all $\mathcal{A}$.
Therefore $\mathcal{A}(\varphi) \neq \mathbf{F}$ for any $\mathcal{A}$,
which means $\mathcal{A}(\neg\varphi) = \mathbf{F}$ for all $\mathcal{A}$.

\textbf{Step 3: Conclude.}

Since $\neg\varphi$ evaluates to $\mathbf{F}$ under every truth-value assignment,
$\neg\varphi$ satisfies the definition of a contradiction.

The converse follows by the same argument with the roles of $\varphi$ and $\neg\varphi$
exchanged, using the fact that $\neg(\neg\varphi) \equiv \varphi$.

\textcolor{darkgreen}{\textbf{Conclusion:}} $\varphi$ is a tautology if and only if
$\neg\varphi$ is a contradiction. \qed

\vspace{0.5cm}

section: Logical Equivalences and Laws of Logic
title: Definition 1.15 --- Logical Equivalence
content:
Two compound propositions $\varphi$ and $\psi$ are \textbf{logically equivalent},
written $\varphi \equiv \psi$, if they have \textbf{identical truth values} for every
possible truth-value assignment of their variables.

\vspace{0.4cm}
\textcolor{primaryblue}{\textbf{\faInfoCircle\ Key Points:}}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.5em]
    \item $\varphi \equiv \psi$ if and only if $\varphi \leftrightarrow \psi$ is a
          \textbf{tautology}.
    \item The symbol $\equiv$ means ``logically equivalent'' ---
          it is \textbf{not} the same as $\leftrightarrow$ (which is a connective inside logic).
    \item Logical equivalence is an \textbf{equivalence relation}: it is reflexive,
          symmetric, and transitive.
    \item We can \textbf{substitute} one side for the other inside any larger formula
          without changing its truth value.
\end{itemize}

\vspace{0.5cm}

section: Logical Equivalences and Laws of Logic
title: Theorem 1.3 --- Laws of Propositional Logic
content:
The following logical equivalences hold for all propositions $p$, $q$, and $r$.
These are the fundamental laws used to simplify compound propositions.

\vspace{0.4cm}
\textbf{Identity Laws:}
\[
    p \land \mathbf{T} \equiv p \qquad\qquad p \lor \mathbf{F} \equiv p
\]

\textbf{Domination Laws:}
\[
    p \lor \mathbf{T} \equiv \mathbf{T} \qquad\qquad p \land \mathbf{F} \equiv \mathbf{F}
\]

\textbf{Idempotent Laws:}
\[
    p \lor p \equiv p \qquad\qquad p \land p \equiv p
\]

\textbf{Double Negation Law:}
\[
    \neg(\neg p) \equiv p
\]

\textbf{Commutative Laws:}
\[
    p \lor q \equiv q \lor p \qquad\qquad p \land q \equiv q \land p
\]

\textbf{Associative Laws:}
\[
    (p \lor q) \lor r \equiv p \lor (q \lor r)
\]
\[
    (p \land q) \land r \equiv p \land (q \land r)
\]

\textbf{Distributive Laws:}
\[
    p \lor (q \land r) \equiv (p \lor q) \land (p \lor r)
\]
\[
    p \land (q \lor r) \equiv (p \land q) \lor (p \land r)
\]

\textbf{De Morgan's Laws:}
\[
    \neg(p \land q) \equiv \neg p \lor \neg q
\]
\[
    \neg(p \lor q) \equiv \neg p \land \neg q
\]

\textbf{Absorption Laws:}
\[
    p \lor (p \land q) \equiv p \qquad\qquad p \land (p \lor q) \equiv p
\]

\textbf{Negation Laws:}
\[
    p \lor \neg p \equiv \mathbf{T} \qquad\qquad p \land \neg p \equiv \mathbf{F}
\]

\textbf{Contrapositive Law:}
\[
    p \rightarrow q \;\equiv\; \neg q \rightarrow \neg p
\]

\textbf{Exportation Law:}
\[
    (p \land q) \rightarrow r \;\equiv\; p \rightarrow (q \rightarrow r)
\]

\vspace{0.5cm}

title: Example 8: Associative Law --- Past Paper 2021 Q1(iii)
content:
State the associative law of union for three sets and verify it logically.

\vspace{0.3cm}
\textcolor{primaryblue}{\textbf{Solution:}}

\vspace{0.3cm}
The associative law of union for sets $A$, $B$, $C$ states:
\[
    (A \cup B) \cup C = A \cup (B \cup C)
\]

\textbf{Logical counterpart:} The analogous law for propositions is:
\[
    (p \lor q) \lor r \;\equiv\; p \lor (q \lor r)
\]

\textbf{Verification by truth table} ($n=3$, so $2^3 = 8$ rows):

\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}
\hline
\rowcolor{primaryblue!20}
$p$ & $q$ & $r$ & $p \lor q$ & $(p\lor q)\lor r$ & $q \lor r$ & $p\lor(q\lor r)$ \\
\hline
T & T & T & T & T & T & T \\
\hline
T & T & F & T & T & T & T \\
\hline
T & F & T & T & T & T & T \\
\hline
T & F & F & T & T & F & T \\
\hline
F & T & T & T & T & T & T \\
\hline
F & T & F & T & T & T & T \\
\hline
F & F & T & F & T & T & T \\
\hline
F & F & F & F & F & F & F \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\vspace{0.3cm}
Columns 5 and 7 are identical. \textcolor{darkgreen}{\checkmark}
\[
    \boxed{(p \lor q) \lor r \;\equiv\; p \lor (q \lor r)}
\]

\textcolor{primaryblue}{\textbf{\faLightbulb\ Section 1.3 Summary --- Logical Equivalences \& Laws}}

\vspace{0.4cm}
\textcolor{primaryblue}{\textbf{\faCheckCircle\ Strategy for Algebraic Simplification:}}
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=2em]
    \item Replace conditionals: $p \rightarrow q \equiv \neg p \lor q$.
    \item Apply \textbf{De Morgan's Laws} to push negations inward.
    \item Apply \textbf{Double Negation} to eliminate $\neg\neg$.
    \item Use \textbf{Distributive Laws} to factor or expand.
    \item Use \textbf{Absorption}, \textbf{Idempotent}, and \textbf{Negation Laws} to reduce.
    \item Apply \textbf{Identity} and \textbf{Domination Laws} to reach the simplest form.
\end{enumerate}

\vspace{0.4cm}
\textcolor{primaryblue}{\textbf{\faCheckCircle\ Most Tested Laws (from past papers):}}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|}
\hline
\rowcolor{primaryblue!20}
\textbf{Law} & \textbf{Equivalence} \\
\hline
De Morgan 1 & $\neg(p\land q) \equiv \neg p \lor \neg q$ \\
\hline
De Morgan 2 & $\neg(p\lor q) \equiv \neg p \land \neg q$ \\
\hline
Conditional & $p\rightarrow q \equiv \neg p \lor q$ \\
\hline
Contrapositive & $p\rightarrow q \equiv \neg q \rightarrow \neg p$ \\
\hline
Double Negation & $\neg\neg p \equiv p$ \\
\hline
Biconditional & $p\leftrightarrow q \equiv (p\rightarrow q)\land(q\rightarrow p)$ \\
\hline
XOR--Biconditional & $\neg(p\oplus q) \equiv p\leftrightarrow q$ \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

Theorem 1.5 --- Rules of Inference for Propositional Logic
content:
The following are the fundamental rules of inference. Each is a tautology.

\vspace{0.5cm}

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{|l|c|l|}
\hline
\rowcolor{primaryblue!20}
\textbf{Rule Name} & \textbf{Tautology} & \textbf{Argument Form} \\
\hline
\textbf{Modus Ponens} &
$(p \land (p \rightarrow q)) \rightarrow q$ &
$p,\quad p \rightarrow q \;\therefore\; q$ \\
\hline
\textbf{Modus Tollens} &
$(\neg q \land (p \rightarrow q)) \rightarrow \neg p$ &
$\neg q,\quad p \rightarrow q \;\therefore\; \neg p$ \\
\hline
\textbf{Hypothetical Syllogism} &
$((p{\rightarrow}q)\land(q{\rightarrow}r))\rightarrow(p{\rightarrow}r)$ &
$p{\rightarrow}q,\; q{\rightarrow}r \;\therefore\; p{\rightarrow}r$ \\
\hline
\textbf{Disjunctive Syllogism} &
$((p \lor q) \land \neg p) \rightarrow q$ &
$p \lor q,\quad \neg p \;\therefore\; q$ \\
\hline
\textbf{Addition} &
$p \rightarrow (p \lor q)$ &
$p \;\therefore\; p \lor q$ \\
\hline
\textbf{Simplification} &
$(p \land q) \rightarrow p$ &
$p \land q \;\therefore\; p$ \\
\hline
\textbf{Conjunction} &
$((p) \land (q)) \rightarrow (p \land q)$ &
$p,\quad q \;\therefore\; p \land q$ \\
\hline
\textbf{Resolution} &
$((p\lor q)\land(\neg p\lor r))\rightarrow(q\lor r)$ &
$p\lor q,\; \neg p\lor r \;\therefore\; q\lor r$ \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\vspace{0.5cm}

Definition 1.23 --- Rules of Inference for Quantified Statements
content:
The following rules extend propositional rules of inference to predicate logic.

\vspace{0.4cm}
\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|l|}
\hline
\rowcolor{primaryblue!20}
\textbf{Rule} & \textbf{Form} & \textbf{Meaning} \\
\hline
\textbf{Universal Instantiation} &
$\forall x\, P(x) \;\therefore\; P(c)$ &
If true for all, true for specific $c$ \\
\hline
\textbf{Universal Generalization} &
$P(c) \;\therefore\; \forall x\, P(x)$ &
If true for arbitrary $c$, true for all \\
\hline
\textbf{Existential Instantiation} &
$\exists x\, P(x) \;\therefore\; P(c)$ for some $c$ &
Name the witness $c$ \\
\hline
\textbf{Existential Generalization} &
$P(c) \;\therefore\; \exists x\, P(x)$ &
One example proves existence \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

\vspace{0.4cm}
\textcolor{accentorange}{\textbf{Important:}} Universal Generalization requires
that $c$ be a \textbf{completely arbitrary} element --- no special assumptions
may be made about it. Otherwise the generalization is invalid.

Definition 1.24 --- Direct Proof
Example 1: Direct Proof --- Even Number
content:
\textbf{Theorem:} If $n$ is an even integer, then $n^2$ is also even.

\vspace{0.3cm}
\textcolor{primaryblue}{\textbf{Solution:}}

\vspace{0.3cm}
\textbf{Identify:} $p$ = ``$n$ is even'', \quad $q$ = ``$n^2$ is even.''

\vspace{0.3cm}
\textbf{Proof:}

\textbf{Step 1: Assume $p$.} Let $n$ be an even integer.

\textbf{Step 2: Use the definition.} By definition of even, there exists an integer
$k$ such that:
\[
    n = 2k
\]

\textbf{Step 3: Derive $q$.} Squaring both sides:
\[
    n^2 = (2k)^2 = 4k^2 = 2(2k^2)
\]
Let $m = 2k^2$. Since $k$ is an integer, $m$ is also an integer, and:
\[
    n^2 = 2m
\]
By definition of even, $n^2$ is even.

\textcolor{darkgreen}{\textbf{Conclusion:}} If $n$ is even, then $n^2$ is even. \qed

\vspace{0.5cm}

Definition 1.26 --- Proof by Contradiction (Reductio ad Absurdum)
content:
A \textbf{proof by contradiction} proves a proposition $p$ by:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textbf{Step \arabic*:}, leftmargin=3.5em]
    \item \textbf{Assume} $\neg p$ (the negation of what we want to prove).
    \item \textbf{Derive} a \textbf{contradiction} --- a statement of the form
          $r \land \neg r$, which is always false.
    \item \textbf{Conclude} that $\neg p$ must be false, so $p$ must be true.
\end{enumerate}

\vspace{0.4cm}
\textcolor{primaryblue}{\textbf{\faInfoCircle\ Key Points:}}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.5em]
    \item Based on the tautology: $(\neg p \rightarrow \mathbf{F}) \rightarrow p$.
    \item If assuming $\neg p$ leads to a logical impossibility, then $\neg p$
          is false, so $p$ must be true.
    \item Particularly useful for proving things are \textbf{irrational},
          \textbf{infinite}, or \textbf{unique}.
    \item Always begin: ``\textit{Assume for contradiction that $\neg p$ is true.}''
\end{itemize}

Example 8: Proof by Contradiction --- Big-O --- Past Paper 2020 Q5(a)
content:
Show that $n^2$ is \textbf{not} $O(n)$.

\vspace{0.3cm}
\textcolor{primaryblue}{\textbf{Solution:}}

\vspace{0.3cm}
\textbf{Recall:} $f(n)$ is $O(g(n))$ if there exist positive constants $C$ and $k$ such that:
\[
    f(n) \leq C \cdot g(n) \quad \text{for all } n > k
\]

\textbf{Step 1: Assume for contradiction} that $n^2$ IS $O(n)$.

Then there exist positive constants $C$ and $k$ such that for all $n > k$:
\[
    n^2 \leq C \cdot n
\]

\textbf{Step 2: Derive consequences.}

Dividing both sides by $n$ (valid since $n > 0$):
\[
    n \leq C \quad \text{for all } n > k
\]

\textbf{Step 3: Reach the contradiction.}

This claims $n$ is bounded above by the constant $C$ for all $n > k$. But $n$ grows
without bound --- for any constant $C$, we can choose $n = \lfloor C \rfloor + 1 > k$
(by taking $k$ large enough), giving $n > C$. This contradicts $n \leq C$.

\textcolor{darkgreen}{\textbf{Conclusion:}} $n^2$ is \textbf{not} $O(n)$. \qed

\vspace{0.5cm}

content:
\textcolor{primaryblue}{\textbf{\faLightbulb\ Exam Preparation Tips for Chapter 1}}

\vspace{0.3cm}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.5em]
    \item \textbf{Q1--Q5} target objective-type questions (2 marks each in past papers).
    \item \textbf{Q6--Q10} target 12-mark subjective questions on equivalences and laws.
    \item \textbf{Q11--Q13} cover predicate logic, which appears in both objective and
          subjective parts every year.
    \item \textbf{Q14--Q16} cover rules of inference --- always present in at least one
          subjective question.
    \item \textbf{Q17--Q20} cover all four proof techniques --- induction questions
          appear almost every year; master the template in Definition~1.27.
    \item For induction proofs, always state $P(n)$, prove the base case explicitly,
          state the inductive hypothesis formally, and show every algebra step.
\end{itemize}
